---
title: "Prompting lab: getting good answers, and knowing their limits"
subtitle: "AIM-5 · AIM-2 · about 75 minutes"
---

::: {.callout-note title="What you'll learn"}
By the end of this chapter you will have:

1. Written a five-part prompt and kept it as a template you will use again.
2. Changed one part at a time and seen what each part does to the answer.
3. Run one made-up case twice in one tool, bare and structured, and said what
   the structure improved and what it did not.
4. Checked the one claim a plan depends on against a calculator, a guideline,
   or a drug label.
5. Said what two randomized trials show about physicians who use a language
   model.
:::

**Time.** About 75 minutes: 20 of reading and 55 of doing. The podcast is
optional. Use your university ChatGPT Edu or Microsoft Copilot account; any
free chatbot also works. There is nothing to install. Open a blank document
before you start, for the template and the record you keep at the end.

## Night float, 2:40 a.m.

You are the intern on night float. Your co-intern Sam comes back from seeing a
44-year-old woman in the emergency department. She is three weeks out from
surgery to fix a broken ankle. She has had two days of sharp chest pain that is
worse when she breathes in. Her heart rate is 108, her oxygen saturation is 95
percent, and her right calf is bigger than the left. Sam has already asked the
chatbot on their phone, twice. The first time they typed the question the way
you would say it out loud. The second time, after a lecture on prompting, they
wrote it out properly: who they are, the case in clinical language, exactly
what they want, and the format they want it in.

Sam hands you the phone. "Second one's much better. I'm going to put it in the
note."

::: {.chat-pair}
<div class="chat-pane">
<div class="prompt">44F, 3 wks post ankle ORIF, pleuritic chest pain x2 days, HR 108, sats 95%, right calf swollen. What's going on and what do I do?</div>
<div class="reply">
<p>This presentation is concerning for a pulmonary embolism (PE), especially given the recent surgery, tachycardia, pleuritic pain, and unilateral calf swelling. Other possibilities include pneumonia, musculoskeletal pain, pericarditis, and pneumothorax. I would recommend getting an ECG and chest X-ray, checking a troponin, and ordering a D-dimer; if the D-dimer is negative, PE can be reasonably excluded. If it is elevated, proceed to CT pulmonary angiography. Consider a lower-extremity Doppler ultrasound for the calf swelling. Provide supplemental oxygen as needed and analgesia.</p>
</div>
<div class="fine">Made-up answer, written for this chapter. Not a transcript of any real tool.</div>
</div>
<div class="chat-pane">
<div class="prompt">You are assisting a physician on an overnight admitting service. A 44-year-old woman, three weeks after open reduction and internal fixation of an ankle fracture, presents with two days of pleuritic chest pain. HR 108, BP 122/78, SpO2 95% on room air, afebrile. Right calf circumference 3 cm greater than left. Give a ranked differential with the findings that most support and most oppose each entry, then the single best next diagnostic step. Table, one row per diagnosis.</div>
<div class="reply">
<table>
<tr><th>#</th><th>Diagnosis</th><th>Supports</th><th>Opposes</th><th>Next step</th></tr>
<tr><td>1</td><td>Pulmonary embolism</td><td>Recent surgery, tachycardia, pleuritic pain, unilateral calf swelling</td><td>Normal BP, only mild hypoxaemia</td><td>D-dimer; CT pulmonary angiography if positive</td></tr>
<tr><td>2</td><td>Deep vein thrombosis without PE</td><td>Calf asymmetry, immobility</td><td>Chest symptoms present</td><td>Compression ultrasound</td></tr>
<tr><td>3</td><td>Pneumonia</td><td>Pleuritic pain</td><td>Afebrile, no cough</td><td>Chest X-ray</td></tr>
<tr><td>4</td><td>Pericarditis</td><td>Pleuritic pain</td><td>No positional component described</td><td>ECG</td></tr>
<tr><td>5</td><td>Musculoskeletal</td><td>Recent immobility</td><td>Tachycardia, hypoxaemia</td><td>Diagnosis of exclusion</td></tr>
</table>
<p><b>Overall:</b> PE is most likely. Obtain a D-dimer; a negative result effectively rules out PE in this setting.</p>
</div>
<div class="fine">Made-up answer, written for this chapter. Not a transcript of any real tool.</div>
</div>
:::

Read both before going on. Sam is right that the second answer is better. It
is ranked, it gives the findings for and against each diagnosis, and it names
a next step in every row. That change came from a few extra sentences in the
prompt. Writing those sentences is the skill this chapter teaches.

Both answers also make the same mistake about the D-dimer, and the table makes
it harder to see. By the end of the chapter you will know the line that belongs
in Sam's prompt, and the check that catches the error.

The skill has a name: **prompting**, writing what you type to a language model
so that what comes back is more useful. A **language model** is the program
behind ChatGPT, Copilot, Claude, and Gemini. It produces text one word-piece (a word or
part of a word) at a time, and the words you give it are the only thing it knows about your case.

**It is your job to learn where these tools help your work, and you learn that
by trying.** If you would rather try first and read after, open your chatbot
now and do Part A of the [Do](#do).

## Why this matters

Within three months you will be Sam. You will have a case, a phone, and a
minute, and what you type will change what comes back. In one study of 148 final-year medical students, only 5 percent had
heard the phrase "clinical prompt engineering". The same students were shown
chatbot answers to ten written cases, and five of the answers were deliberately
wrong. The median student caught the wrong ones 56 percent of the time
[@pmid:39915801].

Asking well takes a few minutes to learn, and you will use it every day. It
gets you answers organised the way you think on rounds, that show their
reasoning, and that say what they are missing. Checking is one step in that
routine, not a reason to avoid the tool.

## How it works

### The five-part prompt

Learn the parts, not fixed wording.

| Element | What you write | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Role** | Who the model is helping | "You are assisting a physician preparing for a case discussion." |
| **Context** | The case, in clinical language | "Epigastric pain radiating to the back," not "stomach pain." Vitals, key negatives, medications. |
| **Task** | Exactly what you want | "Give a ranked differential with the three findings that most support and most oppose each entry." |
| **Format** | The shape of the answer | "Table. One row per diagnosis." |
| **Uncertainty** | What to do with gaps | "Where the case lacks information you would need, say what is missing instead of assuming it." |

: The five-part prompt. The last row is the one this chapter thinks most prompts leave out. {#tbl-scaffold}

The first four rows come from a deck of ten prompting rules this course uses
(see [Watch or listen](#watch-or-listen-optional)). Most of the other rules
make Task and Format more precise: refine over several tries, break a big
question into smaller ones, and show one or two examples of what you want.
None of the ten is the fifth row. Models tend to produce a
complete-looking answer from incomplete information. One likely reason is that
complete-looking answers are what most of the text they learned from looks
like. This chapter's claim
is that asking them to name the gap instead is the most useful single line a
clinician can add to a prompt. You will test that claim yourself in the Do.

::: {.callout-tip title="If English is not your first language"}
[The critical appraisal chapter](core-appraisal.qmd) reports a finding that
also applies here. The same tool made up references ten times more often when a
question was phrased the way a patient talks than the way a clinician writes
[@pmid:42232526]. Linguists call this **register**: the way a particular group
of people talks. It is a property of the words, not of the credentials of the
person typing. The Context row of @tbl-scaffold is where you control it.
Write the case the way you would present it on rounds.
:::

### What structure changes, and what it does not

A prompt can change how an answer is **organised**: ranked or not, with
findings for and against, with a next step, with what it does not know. This
is almost entirely under your control. Ask for a table and you get a table.
That is the reliable part of prompting, and it is worth having: an organised
answer is faster to read and easier to check.

A prompt can also, sometimes, change whether an answer is **correct**. These
are two different properties, and they do not change together. Correctness is
limited by two things a prompt does not change: what the model knows, and what
the case contains. A prompt cannot supply the piece of history you left out.

What a structured prompt *can* do is make the model show its reasoning, so
that you can check it. When a Stanford study prompted GPT-4 to imitate styles
of clinical reasoning, diagnostic accuracy did not change, but the reasoning
became something a physician could read and judge [@pmid:38267608]. Studies
that tested prompt templates directly are in Go deeper. Prompt effects on accuracy are real, but they differ from model to model and
they are unstable. Better organisation is the effect that is reliable.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-what-structure-changes
%%| fig-cap: "What each element of a structured prompt changes. Four of the five act on organisation. The fifth, asking the model to name what is missing, is the only one that acts on the gap between the case and the answer. Context can also affect correctness through how the question is worded (see the callout above)."
flowchart LR
  accTitle: What each element of a structured prompt changes
  accDescr: Role, Context, Task, and Format each point to one box, how the answer is organised. Uncertainty, meaning say what is missing, points to a separate box, whether the answer admits what it does not know. A dotted arrow runs from the organisation box to a box for whether the answer is correct, and its label says it does not touch correctness. A second dotted arrow runs from the admits-what-it-does-not-know box to that same correctness box, and its label says it helps you check.
  R[Role] --> O[How the answer is organised]
```

### The error in Sam's answer

Go back to Sam's phone. A negative D-dimer rules out pulmonary embolism only
when the **pretest probability** is low. Pretest probability is how likely the
diagnosis is before you order any test. The original emergency-department
study validated that strategy in patients whose clinical score put them in the
low-probability group [@pmid:11453709]. Sam's patient has had surgery in the
last four weeks, has a heart rate over 100, and has a swollen calf. On the
Wells score, which MDCalc will calculate for you, she is not low probability.
The right next step is imaging, not a D-dimer, because a positive D-dimer would
only delay the scan. Both answers got this wrong. Only one of them put it in a
column headed "Next step" beside a column of supporting findings.

That is why the neat answer needs more care, not less. **Automation bias** is
trusting a machine's suggestion more than it deserves, and even more when the
output looks authoritative. You read the row, you agree with the findings,
and you accept the next step without a separate check.

Two habits would have protected Sam. The fifth line of the prompt gives you a
place to start, but it does not make the model catch its own error. The check
does: test the one claim the plan depends on, here "a negative D-dimer rules it
out", against a source. For Sam, that is the Wells score in MDCalc.

::: {.callout-important title="The one sentence"}
A structured prompt gets you a better-organised answer that is easier to read
and to check. It does not reliably make the answer right. Ask it to say what is
missing, then check the one claim the plan depends on before anything goes out
with your name on it.
:::

### What the trials show about physicians using the tool

How you use the answer matters too, not only how you ask. In a randomized
trial of 50 physicians working through written cases, those given a language
model scored no better than those without it. The model on its own, in an
exploratory comparison, scored 16 points higher [@pmid:39466245]
(@fig-goh-estimates). In a second trial by the same group, on management, 92
physicians with the model scored 6.5 points higher than those without (95
percent CI 2.7 to 10.2). The model alone scored about the same as them (no
significant difference), and the physicians with the model also took about two
minutes longer per case [@pmid:39910272]. [The centaur-or-cyborg
chapter](core-centaur-cyborg.qmd) covers both trials in more detail.

![Two estimates from the same randomized trial. Physicians with the model did
no better than physicians without it; the model alone did. Redrawn for this
chapter from the estimates reported in Goh et al., *JAMA Network Open* 2024
[@pmid:39466245]; the data are the paper's, the drawing is this course's.](../images/goh-2024-redrawn.png){#fig-goh-estimates fig-alt="Dot-and-interval chart with two rows. Top row: physician plus LLM versus conventional resources, plus 2 percentage points, 95 percent confidence interval minus 4 to plus 8, crossing zero. Bottom row: LLM alone versus conventional resources, plus 16 points, interval 2 to 30, not crossing zero."}

## Do

Use your university ChatGPT Edu or Copilot account, and made-up material only.
Sam's question at 2:40 a.m. was about a real patient, typed into a phone; in
this course, do not do that, even with the name taken out. See [the patient
information page](../course/patient-information.qmd).

### Part A: build a prompt that works (about 20 minutes)

Pick something you will need in the next month: a topic you will present on
rounds, a condition you want to explain to patients, or a question you expect
at interviews. Fill in the brackets and run this in a new conversation.

```
You are helping a fourth-year medical student going into [specialty].
Context: I am preparing a five-minute teaching talk on [topic] for
third-year students on their [specialty] rotation. They already know
[what they know].
Task: give me the three points they most need, one common mistake, and
one question to ask them at the end.
Format: a bulleted list, under 200 words.
Where you are unsure, or where guidelines differ or have changed
recently, say so instead of picking one.
```

Then change one part at a time, each in a new conversation, and compare:

1. Change the **context**: make the audience patients, or an attending.
2. Change the **format**: a table, one paragraph, or three slides.
3. Delete the **last line**. What disappeared from the answer?

Write one line for each change: what it did. Keep the version you liked best.
That is the start of your template.

### Part B: one case, two prompts (about 30 minutes)

You will run one made-up case twice, score both answers, and check the one
claim the plan depends on. Use the same chatbot for both runs, in two separate
conversations, so the second run cannot see the first.

#### Step 1. Pick a case (2 minutes)

Choose by the specialty you plan to enter, or the one whose trap you least
expect to catch. Each case has one deliberate trap. The traps are of different
kinds, and you will not be told which kind yours is until Step 4.

::: {.callout-note title="Case A: emergency medicine or internal medicine"}
A 31-year-old woman presents with two days of right-sided chest pain that is
sharp and worse on inspiration, and shortness of breath when climbing stairs.
Heart rate 102, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation
96 percent on room air, temperature 37.1 °C. Lungs are clear. No cough, no
haemoptysis, no leg swelling or calf tenderness. She describes herself as
otherwise healthy and takes no regular medication that she mentions. She has
not travelled recently.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Case B: internal medicine, family medicine, or geriatrics"}
An 82-year-old woman is brought from an assisted-living facility with two days
of fluctuating confusion; staff say she is "not herself" and was found wandering
at night. Temperature 36.9 °C, heart rate 84, blood pressure 138/78, oxygen
saturation 97 percent. She is inattentive and disoriented to time but has no
focal neurological findings. No dysuria, frequency, or flank pain reported;
no cough. Urine dipstick: leukocyte esterase positive, nitrite positive. White
cell count 8.1. Glucose, sodium, and calcium are normal. Medications:
amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, sertraline 50 mg daily,
acetaminophen as needed, and oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily, started twelve days
ago for urinary urgency.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Case C: surgery, anaesthesia, or any procedural specialty"}
A 66-year-old man attends pre-operative clinic ten days before elective repair
of a right inguinal hernia. Past history: paroxysmal atrial fibrillation,
hyperlipidaemia, type 2 diabetes, and "bronchitis" for which an urgent-care
clinic started an antibiotic last week. Examination is unremarkable apart from
the reducible hernia. Medications: apixaban 5 mg twice daily, amiodarone 200 mg
daily, simvastatin 40 mg nightly, metformin 1000 mg twice daily, tamsulosin 0.4
mg daily, clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily (day 4 of 7). Question for the
model: what needs attention before this operation?
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Case D: psychiatry, neurology, or medicine"}
A 23-year-old man is brought in by his roommate. For ten days he has slept two
to three hours a night without feeling tired, talks rapidly and jumps between
topics, and has spent about $4,000 on equipment for a business he describes in
grand terms. For the last three days he has heard a voice commenting on what he
is doing. Three weeks ago he was started on prednisone 60 mg daily for a severe
contact dermatitis and is now on a taper at 30 mg. No prior psychiatric
history. A maternal uncle has bipolar disorder. He uses cannabis most weekends.
Vital signs and neurological examination are normal.
:::

#### Step 2. The bare prompt (3 minutes)

Paste the case into a new conversation with nothing but this in front of it:

> What's the diagnosis and what should I do?

Copy the whole answer, word for word, into your document under *Bare*. If the
tool replies with questions instead of a plan, do not answer them. The
questions are the answer; copy them and score them like any other reply.

#### Step 3. The structured prompt (5 minutes)

Open a second, new conversation. Here is the five-part template from
@tbl-scaffold; fill in the case where marked.

> You are assisting a physician preparing to present this case at morning
> report. Case: `<paste the case, unchanged>`. Give a ranked differential
> diagnosis with, for each entry, the two or three findings that most support
> it and the two or three that most oppose it, then the single best next step.
> Format as a table, one row per diagnosis, followed by one paragraph on
> management. Where the case lacks information you would need to decide, say
> what is missing instead of assuming it.

Copy the answer word for word under *Structured*. Note the tool and, if it
shows one, the model version.

#### Step 4. Score both (10 minutes)

Now open the trap for your case, below, and score each answer twice: once for
organisation, once for correctness on the trap.

::: {.callout-tip title="The traps, one per case: open only after both runs" collapse="true"}
**Case A: a critical omission.** The case never says whether she is pregnant,
whether she takes hormonal contraception or other oestrogen, whether she has
been immobile, or whether she or her family have had a clot before. Every one
of those changes the pretest probability of pulmonary embolism, and no score
can be computed without them. The trap is whether the model *asks* for them or
*assumes* them. An answer that computes a Wells score, or declares her "low
risk", from what is given has invented the missing history. Full marks require
the answer to name at least two of the missing items as things it needs before
choosing between D-dimer and imaging.

**Case B: the common answer is wrong.** The pattern-match is "urinary tract
infection causing delirium; start antibiotics." But bacteria in the urine
without urinary symptoms is common in older women, especially in care
facilities. The Infectious Diseases Society of America's 2019 guideline
specifically addresses older adults with delirium and no local urinary
symptoms: look for other causes and observe rather than treat the urine
[@pmid:31506700]. The clue that separates the diagnoses is in the medication
list. Oxybutynin is a strongly anticholinergic drug. The American Geriatrics
Society Beers Criteria list it as one to avoid in older adults, and it was
started twelve days before the confusion [@pmid:37139824]. Full marks require
the answer to put the new anticholinergic ahead of, or at least beside, the
dipstick, and to say that the dipstick alone does not establish infection.

**Case C: interactions hidden in the list.** Clarithromycin strongly blocks the
liver enzyme that clears simvastatin. The simvastatin label lists
clarithromycin as a contraindication, and it caps the dose at 20 mg a day with
amiodarone, so 40 mg is over the limit
([DailyMed label](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=4182c956-eb33-1d4b-e054-00144ff88e88)).
The American Heart Association's statement on statin interactions says the
same [@pmid:27754879].
Clarithromycin also raises apixaban exposure through the same pathway, and
amiodarone with clarithromycin puts two QT-prolonging drugs together. The
perioperative apixaban plan and metformin around surgery are the *expected*
content. The trap is whether the model points out the interactions without
being asked. Full marks require the statin-macrolide interaction to be named
and acted on.

**Case D: genuinely ambiguous.** The correct answer is that two diagnoses
remain: corticosteroid-induced mania with psychotic features, and a first
episode of bipolar I disorder with psychotic features, with a cannabis
contribution to exclude. What separates them is time. Symptoms that began
after the steroid started and resolve after it stops point one way; symptoms
that persist point the other. The family history raises the baseline risk
without settling it. Psychiatric effects of corticosteroids are common,
dose-related, usually early in a course, and usually resolve with reduction or
withdrawal [@pmid:17036562]. A model that declares "bipolar I disorder" as
*the* diagnosis has decided too early. Full marks require both diagnoses to
stay on the list with the distinguishing test named, and a safety plan that
does not depend on which it is.
:::

**Organisation, 0 to 5.** One point for each: ranked; findings for *and*
against each entry; an explicit next step; a format you could read aloud on
rounds; a statement of what information is missing.

**Correctness on the trap, 2/1/0.**

| Score | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **2** | The trap is caught and it changes the plan |
| **1** | The trap is mentioned but hidden, softened, or does not change the plan |
| **0** | The trap is missed, or the answer invents around it |

: Scoring correctness on the trap. The scale has only three steps on purpose; arguing with yourself about a borderline case is part of the exercise. {#tbl-trap-score}

#### Step 5. Check the claim the plan depends on (10 minutes)

Take the better of your two answers and find the one claim its plan depends
on: a threshold, a first-line drug, a "rules out", an interaction, a dose.
Check it against one source, in a browser:

- **A calculator or score:** MDCalc, for anything with a score or a threshold.
- **A guideline:** search PubMed with
  `<condition> AND (guideline[Publication Type] OR "practice guideline")`,
  filtered to the last ten years, and take the society's guideline, not a
  commentary on it.
- **A drug label:** DailyMed (<https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov>), the FDA's
  label repository, for any interaction, contraindication, or dose.

Record it as *supported*, *contradicted*, or *not addressed*, with the source.
"Not addressed" is a real result. A claim the sources do not make is a claim
you should not be repeating either. Another chatbot is not a source.

### What you keep (5 minutes)

Fill this in and paste it into this week's [learning
journal](../course/learning-journal.qmd). The top half is a template you can
reuse on any task.

```
MY PROMPT TEMPLATE (the version from Part A I will use again)
Role:      __________________________________________________
Context:   __________________________________________________
Task:      __________________________________________________
Format:    __________________________________________________
Missing:   Where the case lacks information you would need,
           say what is missing instead of assuming it.
           (or your Part A last line)

ONE CASE, TWO PROMPTS (Part B)
Tool: ____________________   Model version if shown: ____________
Case:  A / B / C / D
                       Bare     Structured
Organisation (0–5)     ___      ___
Trap (2/1/0)           ___      ___

The claim the plan depends on: __________________________________
  Source: ______________________   Supported / Contradicted / Not addressed

In one sentence: what did structure change, and what did it not change?
______________________________________________________________________
```

If your organisation score rose and your trap score did not, you have seen the
main point of this chapter yourself. If both rose, write down which sentence
did it; this chapter's guess is the last one. If the bare answer caught the
trap and the structured one did not, keep both transcripts. One case is two
observations, not a study, because the same prompt does not give the same
answer twice [@pmid:38378899].

## Check

Score yourself against this before moving on.

| You have | Meets | Falls short |
|---|---|---|
| A kept template (objective 1) | All five parts of @tbl-scaffold, and you can say which line is the fifth and what it is for | Four parts, or the fifth is "be accurate" |
| Parts changed one at a time (objective 2) | One line each on what changing the context, the format, and the last line did | One run, no changes |
| Two scored answers (objective 3) | Organisation and trap scored separately, the kind of trap named, and a one-sentence finding that names what changed and what did not | One overall impression of which answer was "better" |
| One checked claim (objective 4) | A named calculator, guideline, or label, and a verdict | "It matched what I remembered", or a second chatbot |
| The two trials (objective 5) | The direction of both trials, the model-alone result, and what that implies about where the weak point is | "Studies show AI helps doctors" or "studies show it doesn't" |

## What this changes for you

*What does this change about how you'll practice?* Write it down before you
close the chapter. Two specifics.

First, it is 2:40 a.m. again. Sam holds out the phone: "Second one's much
better. I'm going to put it in the note." Answer Sam in three sentences. Say
what really is better about the second answer, what you would check before it
goes in the note, which line you would add to the prompt next time, and what
you would say about typing a real patient into the phone.

Second, name one task in your own work next week where you will use the
template you kept. Then name the one claim in that task you would check, and
the source you would check it against.

## Summary

- A five-part prompt (role, context, task, format, and "say what is missing")
  reliably gets you a better-organised answer. Keep one as a template.
- Structure does not reliably make the answer correct. Check the one claim the
  plan depends on against a calculator, a guideline, or a label.
- Write the case the way you would present it on rounds.
- In two randomized trials, physicians with a model did not beat the model
  alone. How you use the answer is part of the skill.

## Go deeper

**Papers**

- The randomized trials of physicians with a model: diagnosis [@pmid:39466245]
  and management [@pmid:39910272]. Read the discussion sections for the
  authors' own account of why the benefit did not appear. Both are [the
  centaur-or-cyborg chapter](core-centaur-cyborg.qmd)'s main papers.
- A trial in *NEJM AI* randomized 44 physicians who had just finished a
  20-hour AI-literacy course. When the model's suggestion was wrong, their
  diagnostic scores fell by about 14 points, so the training did not remove
  the automation bias [@doi:10.1056/AIoa2501001]
  [VERIFY: the numbers come from the preprint listing and a search summary; the NEJM AI page blocked the tool on 2026-09-08]{.verify}.
- A single-centre observational study in which pharmacists ran 50
  internal-medicine cases through ChatGPT and OpenEvidence, with and without a
  prompt template. The template made no significant difference to accuracy and
  completeness: the probability of an acceptable answer went from 0.54 to 0.60
  for ChatGPT and from 0.64 to 0.52 for OpenEvidence [@pmid:42324177].
- An orthopaedics study that asked several models about osteoarthritis
  guideline recommendations in several prompt styles. The best style depended
  on the model, and the same question asked five times gave answers whose
  agreement with each other ranged from none to near-perfect [@pmid:38378899].
- A low-back-pain study in which targeted safety prompts improved the weaker
  model on every measure, and the stronger model on everything except safety
  [@pmid:42266874].
- Diagnostic-reasoning prompts as a route to checkable answers
  [@pmid:38267608], and the psychiatry group's prompt built from reusable
  parts, where structure *did* improve the weaker model's accuracy at pulling
  facts out of text [@pmid:42350611]: the counter-example that limits this
  chapter's claim.
- When 33 physicians across 17 specialties graded chatbot answers to 284 of
  their own questions, the median answer was almost completely correct, but 36
  answers were mostly or completely wrong, in the same confident prose as the
  rest [@pmid:37782499].
- When oncologists checked chatbot cancer-treatment recommendations against
  guidelines, about a third of outputs mixed at least one non-guideline
  recommendation in among correct ones [@pmid:37615976].
- The student error-catching study behind the 56 percent [@pmid:39915801]
  (also in [the appraisal chapter](core-appraisal.qmd)), and the published,
  reusable case-based LLM workshop from Harvard [@pmid:42483714]; this
  chapter's Part B is a shorter version of it.
- A tutorial on prompt engineering written for health professionals, for the
  ten-rules material in article form [@pmid:37792434].
